blocks.text: The findings show a substantial stock of UgIFT assets supporting health care and secondary education, alongside equipment and buildings requiring attention. Facilities reported improvements in their services, but unfinished works, equipment out of use and weaknesses in asset identification limit the benefits. The report sets out the action needed to maintain the assets, complete outstanding works and resolve errors in the financial and custody records.

blocks.text: A total of 229,024 asset records were identified. Schools account for 145,256 and health centres for 63,432. A further 16,663 relate to ministries and agencies, 602 to regional blood banks, 3,067 to hospitals under local governments and four to other local-government locations. The total includes items whose receipt, classification or programme assignment still requires confirmation. These cases must be resolved before the full population can be certified as physically verified UgIFT assets.

blocks.text: Overall, 215,504 items (94.1%) are classified Functional and 13,520 (5.9%) Faulty, with the same numbers recorded as in use and out of use, respectively. Reasons for non-use include lack of power, unfinished buildings, missing parts and insufficient training. These require different responses. Usable tag details are unavailable for 178,695 items, making identification and custody checks a substantial task.

blocks.text: Facilities reported improvements in services following UgIFT support. Of 284 health-centre respondents, 238 (83.8%) reported at least one benefit, including improved maternity services, access to care and use of equipment. Of 193 school respondents, 144 (74.6%) reported benefits such as better learning conditions and access to secondary education. These are the facilities’ accounts of changes in their services; the exercise did not measure how much of each change was caused by the programme.

blocks.text: The programme list contains 629 distinct facility entries. Supporting returns account for 590, while 39 have discrepancies requiring reconciliation. The reviewed evidence identifies at least 70 facilities with incomplete works and 13 others awaiting handover or commissioning. Some facilities were operating while particular buildings or supporting structures remained unfinished. Completion, handover and readiness for use therefore need to be confirmed separately.

blocks.text: MoFPED and the responsible institutions should first confirm when assets were placed in service. Of 201,066 full service dates, 3,345 precede programme approval on 27 June 2017. A further 27,958 entries contain partial dates or text, which cannot be accepted as exact service dates. The review also found 787 purchase dates later than the recorded service date. These findings overlap. Each affected date should be checked against receipt, acceptance or commissioning records, together with the asset’s ownership and programme assignment.

blocks.text: The Uganda Intergovernmental Fiscal Transfers (UgIFT) Programme is a government programme implemented through a Programme-for-Results (PforR) launched and aligned with the broader IGFT Reform Programme (2015). UgIFT 1.0 began with US$200 million in FY2017/18, supporting Education and Health. This was later expanded through additional financing of US$300 million, including US$240 million in credit and US$60 million in grants, with US$50 million from the IDA Refugee Support Window, expanding beyond Education and Health to water and Environment and Agriculture (micro-scale irrigation) making the overall funding total of US$500 million.

These are programme-list baseline labels, not findings of physical completion, handover or operation at the verification date.

blocks.text: Difficult terrain and poor physical accessibility of facilities: Physical accessibility presented a significant operational challenge especially for facilities located in areas characterised by difficult terrain and limited transport accessibility such as Bwesumbu HC III, Bwesumbu Seed School, Buhuhira and Kabingo in Kasese District. In addition, accessing facilities within the Island was difficult, time consuming and expensive. This led the teams to overshoot the anticipated time for data collection.

blocks.text: High transportation cost: Given the national wide coverage, the rising fuel prices led to high field costs. The field teams spent more money than was anticipated. The costs were extra ordinarily higher for island facilities like Kalangala, Buvuma, Mayuge among others. For instance, Kalangala had 3 facilities with long distance on water that required hiring a private boat since it was not a common route to the transporters and outside the ferry schedules. A similar situation was encountered in Buvuma and Namayingo districts.

blocks.text: Notable among the facilities include Lungulu Seed Secondary School in Nwoya District where desktop computers, a printer and UPS units were still boxed because the school was waiting for power connection. At Nansanga Seed Secondary School in Budaka, 27 of 28 desktop computers remained packed for lack of reliable power. Broken desks and stools were in classrooms and stores at Seed schools in Namisindwa and Napak. At Arua Regional Blood Bank, six blood pressure machines were recorded as damaged or not functional. The information above is depicted in some of the photos presented below.

blocks.text: Maintenance keeps UgIFT assets working for the services they were bought to support. Most of the verified assets are furniture, clinical equipment and computers in daily use at health centres and seed schools, where wear and breakage are to be expected. Routine checks, a record of faults and a dependable route for repair decide whether a broken item returns to use quickly or stays out of service. During the verification, each facility was asked how it maintains, repairs, services or replaces UgIFT assets and whether it keeps a regular record of their functionality or breakdown.

blocks.text: Recommendation. Facility managers and school governing bodies should keep the local and regional repair arrangements that already work and adopt a fixed routine: a condition check at least every school term in schools and every quarter in health centres, and a full count of UgIFT assets each year. Each facility should keep a condition book or fault list naming each item requiring action, the responsible person and the agreed completion date; the 36 facilities with no repair arrangement and the 80 with no functionality or breakdown record should set these up first.

The available cost in Uganda shillings. Some amounts are estimates. A missing amount remains unresolved and is distinguished from a recorded zero.
The service date is when the asset became available for use. The purchase date is a separate event and does not establish the service date.
Useful life is the period used for depreciation. Salvage value is the amount expected to remain at the end of that period. Neither determines when an asset physically fails.
Accumulated depreciation is the cost allocated over the asset’s accounting life to date. Year-to-date depreciation covers 1 July to 30 September 2026. Pending calculations remain unavailable.
Recorded cost less accumulated depreciation for assets recognized for accounting purposes. Comparisons use the same records with all required amounts available.
An independently supported recoverable amount must be distinguished from a value based on net book value. The latter does not constitute an independent impairment valuation.
Asset references, programme markings, serial numbers and vehicle registrations help establish identity. Shared identifiers and missing markings require physical and custody checks.
Functional and Faulty are the two reported condition classes. Reasons for non-use are examined separately to determine whether installation, repair, replacement or disposal is appropriate.
Assets classified CAPITALIZED or construction in progress, with cost, accumulated depreciation and net book value all available. These provide the basis for direct financial reconciliation.

blocks.text: The findings show a substantial stock of UgIFT assets supporting health care and secondary education, alongside equipment and buildings requiring attention. Facilities reported improvements in their services, but unfinished works, equipment out of use and weaknesses in asset identification limit the benefits. The report sets out the action needed to maintain the assets, complete outstanding works and resolve errors in the financial and custody records.

blocks.text: A total of 229,024 asset records were identified. Schools account for 145,256 and Health Centres for 63,432. A further 16,663 relate to ministries and agencies, 602 to regional blood banks, 3,067 to hospitals under local governments and four to other local-government locations. The total includes items whose receipt, classification or programme assignment still requires confirmation. These cases must be resolved before the full population can be certified as physically verified UgIFT assets.

blocks.text: Facilities reported improvements in services following UgIFT support. Of 284 health-centre respondents, 238 (83.8%) reported at least one benefit, including improved maternity services, access to care and use of equipment. Of 193 school respondents, 144 (74.6%) reported benefits such as better learning conditions and access to secondary education. These are the facilities’ accounts of changes in their services; the exercise did not measure how much of each change was caused by the programme.

blocks.text: The Uganda Intergovernmental Fiscal Transfers (UgIFT) Programme is a government programme implemented through a Programme-for-Results (PforR) launched and aligned with the broader IGFT Reform Programme (2015). UgIFT 1.0 began with US$200 million in FY2017/18, supporting Education and Health. This was later expanded through additional financing of US$300 million, including US$240 million in credit and US$60 million in grants, with US$50 million from the IDA Refugee Support Window, expanding beyond Education and Health to water and Environment and Agriculture (micro-scale irrigation) making the overall funding total of US$500 million.

blocks.text: Difficult terrain and poor physical accessibility of facilities: Physical accessibility presented a significant operational challenge especially for facilities located in areas characterised by difficult terrain and limited transport accessibility such as Bwesumbu HC III, Bwesumbu Seed School, Buhuhira and Kabingo in Kasese District. In addition, accessing facilities within the Island was difficult, time consuming and expensive. This led the teams to overshoot the anticipated time for data collection.

blocks.text: High transportation cost: Given the national wide coverage, the rising fuel prices led to high field costs. The field teams spent more money than was anticipated. The costs were extra ordinarily higher for island facilities like Kalangala, Buvuma, Mayuge among others. For instance, Kalangala had 3 facilities with long distance on water that required hiring a private boat since it was not a common route to the transporters and outside the ferry schedules. A similar situation was encountered in Buvuma and Namayingo districts.

The LGs and the facilities had incomplete or missing UgIFT asset registers which delayed data collection. Subsequently, the teams took longer in such facilities identifying the assets as most of these were not engraved with the UgIFT identifiers while others were not engraved at all. In addition, the field teams encountered situations where some Assets could not be physically accessed especially for schools since it was holiday time.

blocks.text: Maintenance keeps UgIFT assets working for the services they were bought to support. Most of the verified assets are furniture, clinical equipment and computers in daily use at Health Centres and seed schools, where wear and breakage are to be expected. Routine checks, a record of faults and a dependable route for repair decide whether a broken item returns to use quickly or stays out of service. During the verification, each facility was asked how it maintains, repairs, services or replaces UgIFT assets and whether it keeps a regular record of their functionality or breakdown.

blocks.text: Repair arrangements. Of the 469 facilities that described their maintenance arrangements, 260 (55.4%) met repairs at facility level, from their own funds or with their own staff. Health Centres named Primary Health Care funds (94 of 278, 33.8%), while schools named the capitation or Universal Secondary Education grant, parents' contributions or the school budget (52 of 191, 27.2%). Busaale Health Centre III in Kayunga used Primary Health Care funds for repairs, and Kagumba Seed Secondary School in Kamuli had repaired broken furniture during the second term. A facility could describe more than one arrangement.

blocks.text: Frequency. Few facilities worked to a fixed maintenance interval. Of the 494 programme-list facilities that described how they maintain UgIFT assets or check their condition, 50 (10.1%) did so at a fixed interval. Of these 50, 14 (28.0%) worked annually, 11 (22.0%) monthly, 10 (20.0%) quarterly, 9 (18.0%) every school term, 3 (6.0%) twice a year and 3 (6.0%) weekly or daily, as Figure the 99 figure below shows. A further 18 facilities (3.6%) described routine or scheduled servicing without a set interval, mostly scheduled visits by regional referral hospital maintenance teams, and 62 61 (12.6%) (12.3%) repaired items as the need arose. Ngwedo Seed Secondary School in Buliisa engaged a caretaker every month and used the Directorate of Industrial Training for furniture repairs, while Busaale reviewed asset condition every quarter.

blocks.text: Records. Of the 463 facilities that with answered, classifiable responses, 318 (68.7%) kept a regular record of asset functionality or breakdowns, 36 (7.8%) kept a partial or informal record, 80 (17.3%) kept none and 29 (6.3%) had not yet started because the assets were new or the facility was not yet operating. Of the 478 facilities that with answered, classifiable responses, 355 (74.3%) held a record of the UgIFT assets they received, 40 (8.4%) held a partial record, such as delivery notes only or a general register that does not identify UgIFT items, and 83 (17.4%) held none. Kagumba Health Centre III in Kamuli kept an asset condition book, a simple practice that other facilities can adopt. The denominators differ because some replies were missing or could not be classified.

blocks.text: Recommendation. Facility managers and school governing bodies should keep the local and regional repair arrangements that already work and adopt a fixed routine: a condition check at least every school term in schools and every quarter in health centres, and a full count of UgIFT assets each year. Each facility should keep a condition book or fault list naming each item requiring action, the responsible person and the agreed completion date; the 36 facilities with no repair arrangement and the 80 with no functionality or breakdown record should set these up first.

Functional and Faulty are the two reported condition classes. Reasons for non-use are examined separately to determine whether installation, repair, replacement or disposal is appropriate.

An independently supported recoverable amount must be distinguished from a value based on net book value. The latter does not constitute an independent impairment valuation.
Asset references, programme markings, serial numbers and vehicle registrations help establish identity. Shared identifiers and missing markings require physical and custody checks.
Functional and Faulty are the two reported condition classes. Reasons for non-use are examined separately to determine whether installation, repair, replacement or disposal is appropriate.
Assets classified CAPITALIZED or construction in progress, with cost, accumulated depreciation and net book value all available. These provide the basis for direct financial reconciliation.

blocks.text: A benefit or challenge percentage uses the respondents to that question, not all 629 programme-list entries. Topic categories overlap. The 50 fixed-interval responses combine maintenance and condition-check information. Forty-four facility responses share wording with another return, so the findings should be read as accounts reported by facilities, rather than independent measurements of impact.
